## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should have:

- **git installed** and set up with your name and email,
- turned a small practice project into a **git repository**, with a `.gitignore` that keeps a (fake) secret out,
- made **commits with messages** that read like lab-notebook entries,
- asked **"what changed?"** and read a diff, including a change you did not want,
- **undone a bad agent edit** with git, and checked that nothing else was lost,
- **read the history** of the project as a short table, and
- done the same for **your own project folder**, which is from now on a git repository.

You never type a git command yourself. The agent does that; you read what it proposes, approve it, and check the result.

Your session will look different from anyone else's, including the examples below. Compare **results**, not sessions.

## Before you start

- You have done *Organising a project for an agent*: your own project folder has its structure and a `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`.
- You know how to start the agent in a folder and read permission requests (*Terminal survival kit*).
- Download the practice project: [plate-growth.zip](data/plate-growth.zip). It holds a tiny synthetic experiment: optical density readings of 12 plates, a script `clean.py` that summarises them, a lab note, and a file `.env` with a **fake** secret.
- Unzip it into your course folder, so you get `~/agentic-course/git-basics/plate-growth/` (Windows: `C:\Users\<you>\agentic-course\git-basics\plate-growth\`). On Windows, check that you did not get `plate-growth\plate-growth\`.
- The file `.env` starts with a dot, so your file browser may hide it. That is normal. (Mac Finder: **Cmd+Shift+.** shows hidden files. Windows Explorer: **View → Show → Hidden items**.)

### Starting the agent

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Claude Code
```bash
cd ~/agentic-course/git-basics/plate-growth
claude
```
Keep **manual mode** for this exercise (the status line below the prompt box; **Shift+Tab** cycles), so you see every git command before it runs.

## Codex
```bash
cd ~/agentic-course/git-basics/plate-growth
codex
```
The folder is not yet a git repository, so Codex will probably suggest **Read Only**. To let it create the repository, type `/permissions` and choose the level that lets it edit files in the workspace (not full access). After the repository exists, a new Codex session in this folder will suggest **Auto**. Check with `/status`.
:::

## Worked example

### Step 1: Check git, and install it if needed

```text
Is git installed on this computer, and which version? Only check,
do not install anything.
```

If git is missing, ask for a plan, read it, and approve step by step:

```text
Git is missing. Suggest how to install it on this computer, using the
official source or the usual package manager. Show me the plan first
and tell me which steps need my password or a system window.
```

| System | What usually happens |
|---|---|
| Mac | A system window offers to install the Command Line Tools, which include git. Click **Install**. Or the agent uses Homebrew if you have it. |
| Windows | Git for Windows from [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win), or `winget`. Accept the default choices. Then **close and reopen the terminal**. |
| Linux | The package manager (`apt`, `dnf`); you type your password. |
| Managed laptop | If installing is blocked, use the software centre or ask IT. |

Then let git know who you are:

```text
Check whether git knows my name and email. If not, set them for my user
account. Ask me which name and email to use; do not guess.
```

**What to look for.** The agent runs something like `git config --global user.name` and `user.email`. These only affect git on your computer. The name and email go into every commit you make from now on (see the lecture for the privacy point).

### Step 2: Make the project a repository, ignore list first

Look at the folder in your file browser for a minute first (with hidden files shown). Then:

```text
Make this folder a git repository. Before the first commit:
1. create a .gitignore that keeps out secrets (such as .env), system
   junk files and anything large or personal you see;
2. list every file you are about to commit and flag anything that looks
   like a secret, personal data or a large file.
Then commit everything else with a message saying what the project
contains. Show me the message before you commit.
```

**What to look for.** The order: `git init`, then `.gitignore`, then the list of files, then the commit. Read the file list before you approve the commit.

#### Check the result

1. Ask: "**Is .env in any commit? Show me the list of files in the last commit.**" `.env` must **not** be in the list. `.gitignore` should be.
2. The commit contains **6 files**: `.gitignore`, `README.md`, `clean.py`, `data/raw/plates.csv`, `notes/2026-11-20.md`, `results/summary.csv`. (If the agent chose to ignore `results/` because the script can remake it, you get 5. That is a defensible choice; ask it to explain.)
3. Open `.gitignore` in a text editor. It names `.env`. It may name other things too; ask about any line you do not understand.
4. In your file browser, a hidden folder `.git` has appeared. Do not open or change it.

### Step 3: A good change, committed with a lab-notebook message

```text
Add a column with the standard deviation (sd_od600_8h) to
results/summary.csv, by changing clean.py and rerunning it.
Change nothing else.
```

When it is done, ask:

```text
What changed since the last commit? List the files, then explain the
changes in plain words.
```

**What to look for.** Two files changed: `clean.py` and `results/summary.csv`. Nothing in `data/raw/`. If anything else changed, ask why.

Open `results/summary.csv`. The means must be unchanged: **control 0.758, glucose 2.654, salt 0.254**, with **n_plates 4, 3, 4** (plate P07 is excluded, see the lab note). There is a new column with three standard deviations.

Now commit:

```text
Commit this. First line: what we did. Then one or two lines: why, and
which files and results it affects. Show me the message first.
```

Read the message. Is every claim in it true? If not, say what is wrong before it commits.

### Step 4: A deliberately bad edit, and the undo

Now we make the kind of mess an agent can make, on purpose, so you can practise getting out of it:

```text
For practice, make a deliberately bad change. Do not commit it.
1. In clean.py, stop excluding plate P07.
2. In data/raw/plates.csv, change plate P05's reading at hour 8 to 2.9.
3. Rerun clean.py.
```

Look at `results/summary.csv`: the glucose mean has jumped (to about **3.2**, with n = 4). Now ask the questions you would ask after any real agent session:

```text
What changed since the last commit? List every file, and tell me if
any raw data changed.
```

**What to look for.** Three files: `clean.py`, `data/raw/plates.csv` and `results/summary.csv`. The raw-data change should stand out. Ask the agent to show you that diff; you see the old line in red and the new line in green.

Now undo it:

```text
Undo all changes since the last commit. Before you do, tell me exactly
what will be thrown away and what will be kept.
```

**What to look for.** The command proposed should be a `git restore` of those files (or something with the same effect). If you see `git reset --hard` or `git clean`, stop and ask what it would delete: here it would be harmless, but it is a good habit.

#### Check the result

1. Ask: "**Is everything committed? Is anything different from the last commit?**" The answer should be that nothing has changed (a "clean working tree").
2. Open `results/summary.csv` (if `results/` is in your `.gitignore`, git cannot restore it: ask the agent to rerun `clean.py` first): glucose is back to **2.654**, n = 3, and your standard deviation column from step 3 is still there. The good change survived; only the bad one went.
3. Open `data/raw/plates.csv` and find `P05,glucose,8,`. The value is **2.659** again.

### Step 5: Undo a commit, keeping the record

Sometimes you notice a mistake only after it was committed. Make a small committed change, then reverse it:

```text
Change clean.py so it summarises hour 6 instead of hour 8, rerun it and
commit with a message. Then undo that commit with a new commit that
reverses it (git revert), so the history keeps both.
```

#### Check the result

- The summary is back at hour 8 (glucose **2.654**).
- Ask for the history. The last two entries are your hour-6 commit and a "Revert ..." commit. The mistake and its correction are both in the notebook.

### Step 6: Read the history

```text
Show me the history of this project as a short table: date, short id,
message. Then tell me: when did we add the standard deviation, and what
did clean.py look like before that?
```

You should see **4 commits** (the first one, the standard deviation, the hour-6 change and its revert) and the old version of `clean.py` without the standard deviation.

### Step 7 (optional): Claude Code checkpoints

In Claude Code, ask for a harmless edit, for example "Add a line 'Practised git on <date>' at the end of README.md." Then type `/rewind` (or press **Esc** twice with an empty prompt), select that prompt, and choose **Restore code**. The line disappears. Ask "is anything different from the last commit?": the answer should be no.

This works only for files Claude edited in this session. Git covers everything. See the [checkpointing documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Expected outcomes for the worked example"}
- First commit: 6 files; `.env` not among them; `.gitignore` names `.env`.
- `results/summary.csv` after step 3: control n = 4, mean 0.758; glucose n = 3, mean 2.654; salt n = 4, mean 0.254; plus a standard deviation column.
- After the bad edit in step 4: glucose n = 4, mean about 3.24 (with P05 at 2.9). After the undo: back to n = 3, mean 2.654, and `P05,glucose,8,2.659` in the raw data.
- History after step 5: 4 commits, the last one a "Revert ..." of the hour-6 commit.
- Your messages will be worded differently. They should each say what was done, and the step-3 message should mention the new column.
:::

## On your own project

Your own project folder becomes a git repository today. From now on, every agent session in it follows the routine: clean start, one task, read the diff, check, commit or undo.

**Privacy first.** Look at the "Data class and precautions" and "Never put in this folder" sections of your README. Anything personal, confidential or secret that is in the folder must go in `.gitignore` **before** the first commit, or better, not be in the folder at all. Once committed, a file stays in the history.

1. Start the agent in your **project folder** (for example `~/agentic-course/soil-funding-map/`), not in the course folder.
2. Make it a repository, ignore list first:

```text
Make this folder a git repository. Before the first commit:
1. read README.md (especially "Data class and precautions" and
   "Never put in this folder") and CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md;
2. create a .gitignore that keeps out secrets, system junk, large files
   and anything the README says must not be shared;
3. list every file you are about to commit, with its size, and flag
   anything that might be personal, confidential or large.
Then commit with a message describing what the project contains so far.
Show me the file list and the message before you commit.
```

3. Read the file list carefully. If something should not be there, say so and have it added to `.gitignore` before the commit.
4. Add the routine to the project's instructions file, so the agent follows it in every session:

```text
Add a short section "Git routine" to CLAUDE.md (or AGENTS.md):
- at the start of a session, check that everything is committed;
- one task at a time; after each task, list the changed files;
- never change files in data/raw;
- commit only when I ask, with a message saying what, why and what it
  affects;
- never run git reset --hard, git clean or git push --force without
  asking me and saying what would be lost.
Commit this change.
```

5. **Bad-edit drill on your own project.** Ask for a small, harmless but unwanted change (for example "add a sentence to the Goal section of README.md that I did not write"). Then: "What changed since the last commit?", and "Undo it; tell me first what will be lost." Check that README.md is back as it was.
6. Add a line to the **Log of AI use** section of your README: today's date, "made the project a git repository; added git routine", and commit it.

### Check the result

- Ask: "**Show me the history as a short table.**" You see at least three commits: the first snapshot, the git routine, and the log entry.
- Ask: "**List every file git is tracking.**" Nothing on it is personal, secret or large. Nothing from your "Never put in this folder" list is on it.
- Ask: "**Is anything not committed?**" The answer should be no.
- If you use Codex, start a new session in the project folder and check with `/status` which level it now suggests (Auto in a git folder). Decide whether that is what you want for this project; if your data is sensitive, stay with Read Only.

## What you should have now

- Git installed, with your name and email set.
- The practice project `plate-growth` with a history of 4 commits, which you have read, diffed and undone.
- **Your own project folder as a git repository**, with a `.gitignore` that matches your data class, a "Git routine" section in `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, and a first few commits whose messages read like a lab notebook.

In *Reproducible figures* you commit your first figure together with the script that makes it. In *GitHub* the history goes online.
